brainstorm-topic: Maya picked her topic in five minutes with ChatGPT. Why is that so tempting when a proposal is due Friday, and what might a writer lose by choosing the topic that sounds easiest to research?
Compare asking AI to poke holes in ideas you already have with asking AI to give you the ideas in the first place. How does the order change whose thinking ends up in the project?
The course policy says your own voice and thinking come first. If AI wrote your working thesis and you logged it honestly, would that thesis still be yours? Why or why not?
research-sources: Why might a writer who feels lost in the library databases be tempted to ask AI for a ready-made list of sources, and what does that list leave out about how research actually works?
What is the difference between annotating an article you read yourself and annotating an AI summary of it? Think of a time a summary of something gave you a different impression than the real thing.
Several choices here involve AI, but they put very different amounts of checking on you. How would you decide what you need to verify yourself before a source goes in your bibliography?
drafting-intro: It is 11 p.m. and a chatbot tab is open. What makes letting AI write the intro feel reasonable in that moment, and what would make you stop and choose something else?

If you have AI draft an intro and then rewrite it heavily, how much of its framing do you think sticks with you? How would you answer the log question about whether the piece would be meaningfully different without AI?
Some writers save the intro for last and build it from their body paragraphs. How does that compare to asking AI to teach you opening strategies, and which would help you more on your next paper?
citations-works-cited: Why might a writer think an MLA citation for a chatbot is enough disclosure? What does a GenAI log entry tell your instructor that a works cited entry does not?
If a statistic came from AI and you never found the original source, what should happen to it in your paper? Talk about how you would handle that with an hour left before the deadline.
Compare using AI to format citations you already gathered with using a citation manager like Zotero. How would you check the results in either case, and what do you learn about MLA along the way?
consequence-missing-source: Why is it so tempting to say the sources are real or quietly swap in new ones when an instructor emails about missing sources? What makes honesty feel risky in that moment?
Several choices here involve fixing the list, but they differ in how much they tell the instructor. Why might the honest account of where the sources came from matter as much as the corrected list?
The policy says the log is not a punishment or a surveillance tool. How could writing a late log entry about this mistake actually help you as a researcher on your next project?
peer-review-classmate: Jordan said "be honest." What kind of feedback can only a human reader give, and why might a classmate want that more than a long list of AI comments?
Jordan shared the draft with you, not with an AI company. How should consent and privacy shape what you do with someone else's writing, and would you want your own draft pasted into a chatbot?

Compare writing your comments first and then asking AI what reviewers often miss with asking AI to explain counterarguments before you read. How would you log either one, and how might each help your own revision?
consequence-pitch: Your topic was picked because it comes from something you have lived. What might be lost if you read an AI-written script about your own experience, and why is that option still tempting with two days to prepare?

Compare having AI draft slides that you rewrite and cut with drafting the pitch yourself and having AI play a skeptical listener. Whose thinking shapes the argument in each case, and what would you put in your GenAI log?

Moving from a paper to a two-minute spoken pitch is a new audience and a new medium. What from your original freewrite or a practice run with a friend would help you most, and could AI give you the same thing?
revising-development: Why might a built-in Rewrite button feel like it does not count as AI? The policy names writing assistants embedded in many platforms, so how would you decide what belongs in your log?
Your instructor asked for more support and analysis, not smoother sentences. What is the difference between polishing a paragraph and developing an idea, and which kinds of help do each?
If you asked AI to point out weak claims, how would you compare its list with your instructor's comments? What might that comparison reveal about how AI reads compared to how a person reads?
consequence-conference: When an instructor asks how you wrote a section, why might a writer be tempted to downplay the tool or deny using AI at all? What does each of those answers do to the conversation?

The instructor noticed some sections did not sound like the rest of your writing. What do you think makes your writing sound like you, and how might comparing your own rewrite with the AI version help you see it?

Compare explaining honestly and completing the missing log entries now with offering to rewrite the sections yourself. What does each one repair, and how does each connect to the policy's idea that the log is a reflection practice?
